title: Renovate and the upgrade fixers

story: It is the 1st of the month, 03:00. Renovate, the bot that proposes dependency updates, opens its monthly frontend PR: nine package updates in one group, each at least a week old. Frontend CI turns red. One test expected the date 2026-10-16 and got 16 Oct 2026. The error names a test, not a package, and nine changelogs could explain it.

Give the whole group to one agent session and it reads nine changelogs, changes code for packages that never broke anything, and returns a fix that nobody can review. A person would do something simpler: put the updates in one at a time until the test breaks. That question, which one broke it, comes before any fix.
hook.question: When a grouped update breaks the build, how does a fixer find the one package that broke it and repair only that?

read.h: Few updates, grouped, a week old
p: Dependency updates are a noise problem before they are a code problem. A bot that opens one PR per package every day trains people to ignore it, the same lesson as the old weekly dependency workflow. So Renovate runs with a slow, grouped pace. New PRs appear only on the 1st of the month. Updates are grouped by the team that reviews them, so the frontend gets one "frontend npm" PR, and the backend guild gets its own. A release must be at least 7 days old before Renovate proposes it, which gives the rest of the world a week to find its bugs. Every major version gets its own PR, because a major is the kind of update most likely to need real work.

Most months, most groups are green, and a person approves them in a minute. The upgrade fixers exist for the few that are red. They are routines: the same agent as Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, started by a failed Renovate PR instead of a ticket, with one run per PR, named upgrade:fcp:pr- and the PR number.

code.text:
{
  extends: ["config:recommended"],
  timezone: "Asia/Jerusalem",
  schedule: ["* 2-6 1 * *"],          // new PRs only on the 1st of the month
  minimumReleaseAge: "7 days",          // nothing younger than a week
  internalChecksFilter: "strict",
  packageRules: [
    { matchFileNames: ["frontend/**"], groupName: "frontend npm", reviewers: ["team:frontend-guild"] },
    { matchFileNames: ["cloud/rhinoCloud/**"], groupName: "cloud python", reviewers: ["team:backend-guild"] },
    { matchUpdateTypes: ["major"], groupName: null },   // every major gets its own PR
  ],
}

notes.text: Between 02:00 and 06:59 on the 1st of each month, Israel time.
A release must be 7 days old before Renovate proposes it.
One group per area, reviewed by the team that owns it.
Majors leave their group, so a fixer can take each one alone.

p: The first step needs no model at all. On the base commit, the main commit the Renovate branch started from, the fixer applies one bump at a time, runs the checks, and throws the bump away again. Nine bumps, nine short runs, and at the end a list: these packages break us, these do not. Usually the list has one name on it. The idea is the same as git bisect, which finds the commit that broke something by testing history step by step, except that here the steps are packages instead of commits.

Only then does a model start, and it starts small. Each breaking package gets its own fix session, one after another, on the base commit with only that one bump applied. The session sees one change and one set of errors. It reads that package's changelog and migration guide, searches our code for every use of the package, tries the package's codemod if it has one (a script that rewrites code for the new version), and runs the end-to-end specs and stories that use it. One small pipeline per package is easier for the model and easier for the reviewer than one big session for the whole group.

notes.text: Step 1: each bump alone, always starting from the same base commit.
Red with only this bump: this package breaks us.
Step 2: one fix session per breaking package, one after another, never in parallel.
A package it cannot fix goes to a person, with notes on what breaks and why.
Step 3: the real Renovate branch with every bump, plus every fix commit.
Pushed to the Renovate branch through the broker's git proxy, which allows only that branch.

p: Fixes that pass one by one can still clash, so the last step checks them together: the fixer takes the real Renovate branch with all nine bumps, adds every fix commit on top, and runs the checks again, including the flows that use each package. Green means the fix commits are pushed to the Renovate branch itself, through the broker's git proxy (the service that holds our GitHub credentials and pushes only to the branch a run is allowed to touch). The group stays one PR with the repair inside it. Renovate sees that someone edited its branch and stops rebasing it, which is what we want. The PR carries the routine's label and its owner's Requested-by: line, so a person who did not ask for it approves it.

Some answers are not fixes. If the fixes clash, or a package cannot be made to work, the fixer comments on the PR with what breaks and why, and a person decides. It never pins the old version back and calls that a fix, because that only undoes the update and hides the problem until next month. And the gRPC and protobuf packages always go to the backend guild, because they are the contract between our cloud and client, and changing them is a people decision.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the backend and infrastructure fixers
p: The backend upgrade fixer, a routine for Python updates in cloud, client and the SDK, uses the same three steps. Its charter, the routine's reviewed settings file, names the exact command that bumps one package in each folder, for example uv lock --upgrade-package for cloud, followed by make update-deps so the integration-test requirements stay in step, and uv pip compile for the SDK. Its done list adds the SDK tests and an OpenAPI diff that must show no unplanned API change.

The infrastructure upgrade fixer repairs Renovate PRs for OpenTofu providers, Helm charts and GitHub Action pins. In the infrastructure repo, provider versions sit inside a multi-line string in common.hcl files, where Renovate's normal Terraform reader cannot see them, so a custom regex manager reads them instead, and chart versions are found through a # renovate: marker line above each default. The fixer checks its work without any cloud credentials (format, validate without a backend, tflint, trivy, helm template into kubeconform) and never applies anything; a person reads the plan and applies.

lab.title: Which package broke it?
lab.goal: Make a grouped update that breaks one test, find the one package that broke it by trying each bump alone, fix only that package, and check all fixes together.

guess.q: The group updates three packages, @lab/dates, @lab/numbers and @lab/strings, and a test now prints 16 Oct 2026 instead of 2026-10-16. How should the fixer find the package that broke it?

options.text: Ask one agent session to read all three changelogs and change the code.
options.why: With nine or ten packages, that session guesses and changes code for packages that never broke anything.

options.text: Apply each bump alone on main and run the tests, so only the breaking package fails.
options.why: That is step 1. It needs no model and turns a group into a short list of culprits.

options.text: Pin all three packages back to their old versions.
options.why: That undoes the update instead of repairing it, and the same PR comes back next month.

follow.say: Make three tiny packages, two versions each, packed as tarballs the way a registry serves them. No internet is needed.
follow.do:
mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/g5-6 && cd ~/academy-labs/g5-6
cat > make-packages.sh <<'EOF'
# three tiny packages, two versions each, packed into vendor/ the way a registry would serve them
mkdir -p pkgs vendor
pack() { # name version code
  mkdir -p "pkgs/$1-$2"
  printf '{ "name": "@lab/%s", "version": "%s", "type": "module", "main": "index.js" }\n' "$1" "$2" > "pkgs/$1-$2/package.json"
  printf '%s\n' "$3" > "pkgs/$1-$2/index.js"
  (cd "pkgs/$1-$2" && npm pack --silent --pack-destination ../../vendor > /dev/null)
}
pack dates 1.4.0 'export const formatDate = (d) => d.toISOString().slice(0, 10);'
pack dates 1.5.0 'export const formatDate = (d, style = "short") => style === "iso" ? d.toISOString().slice(0, 10) : d.toLocaleDateString("en-GB", { day: "numeric", month: "short", year: "numeric" });'
pack strings 3.0.1 'export const title = (s) => s.charAt(0).toUpperCase() + s.slice(1);'
pack strings 3.0.2 'export const title = (s) => (s ? s.charAt(0).toUpperCase() + s.slice(1) : s);'
pack numbers 2.3.0 'export const percent = (x) => `${Math.round(x * 100)}%`;'
pack numbers 2.4.0 'export const percent = (x, digits = 0) => `${(x * 100).toFixed(digits)}%`;'
rm -rf pkgs
ls vendor
EOF
bash make-packages.sh

follow.say: Make a small frontend that uses all three packages, with one test, and commit it as a green main.
Now be Renovate: one branch that updates all three packages in one group. CI turns red, and the error names a test, not a package.
follow.do:

npm install --silent ./vendor/lab-dates-1.5.0.tgz ./vendor/lab-strings-3.0.2.tgz ./vendor/lab-numbers-2.4.0.tgz
git commit -qam "chore(deps): update frontend npm (monthly)" && npm test 2>&1 | grep -E "^# fail|expected|actual"

expected: 'Atlas · 2026-10-16 · 40% done'
  actual: 'Atlas · 16 Oct 2026 · 40% done'
# fail 1

follow.say: Go back to main for the next part, so you start from the base commit.
follow.do: git switch -q main && git status --short && echo clean

lab.build: Write ../try-each.sh, then run it from the fcp folder with bash ../try-each.sh. For every dependency on the renovate/monthly branch (read it with git show renovate/monthly:package.json and jq), restore main's package.json and package-lock.json, run npm ci, install that one tarball, run npm test, and print ok or BREAKS with the tarball's name. At the end, restore main's files again. Then repair: make a branch fix/dates from main with only the dates bump, change src/report.js to call formatDate(date, "iso"), and commit the fix separately from the bump. Finally, switch to renovate/monthly, cherry-pick only the fix commit, run npm ci and npm test.
checks: bash ../try-each.sh prints BREAKS for vendor/lab-dates-1.5.0.tgz and ok for the other two.
After the script, git status --short in fcp prints nothing: main's files are back.
On fix/dates, npm test passes with only the dates bump and the one-line change.
On renovate/monthly after the cherry-pick, npm test passes, and git log --oneline main.. shows the update commit and the fix commit.

solution.text:
# Try each bump of the Renovate branch alone, on top of main, and say which ones break the tests.
for bump in $(git show renovate/monthly:package.json | jq -r '.dependencies[] | ltrimstr("file:")'); do
  git checkout -q main -- package.json package-lock.json && npm ci --silent
  npm install --silent "./$bump"
  if npm test --silent > /dev/null 2>&1; then echo "ok      $bump"; else echo "BREAKS  $bump"; fi
done
git checkout -q main -- package.json package-lock.json && npm ci --silent

# then: fix the one package alone, and check all fixes together
git switch -qc fix/dates main && npm install --silent ./vendor/lab-dates-1.5.0.tgz
git commit -qam "chore(deps): bump @lab/dates alone"
sed -i.bak 's/formatDate(date)/formatDate(date, "iso")/' src/report.js && rm src/report.js.bak
npm test && git commit -qam "fix: ask @lab/dates 1.5 for the ISO format"
git switch -q renovate/monthly && git cherry-pick fix/dates && npm ci --silent && npm test

lab.fix: A teammate's version of try-each.sh installs the bumps one after another without restoring main's package.json between them. It prints BREAKS for dates, and then BREAKS for numbers and strings too, so the fixer starts three fix sessions for one broken package. Make that change, see the wrong output, and explain why every bump must start from the same base.
explain: Why does the fixer try each bump alone before any model starts?
Why does each breaking package get its own fix session, and why one after another?
Why is pinning the old version back never a fix?
lab.done: Your script names the one package that broke the group, the one-line fix works alone and together on the Renovate branch, and main stayed untouched.

check.q: A grouped Renovate PR with eight updates is red. Two bumps fail when tried alone on the base commit. How many fix sessions run?

options.text: One, for the whole group, so it sees everything
options.why: One big session mixes eight changes and two sets of errors. That is what the pipeline avoids.

options.text: Eight, one per package, to be safe
options.why: Six packages broke nothing, so they need no session at all.

options.text: Two, one per breaking package, one after another
options.why: Step 1 found two culprits. Each gets a small session with only its own bump.

check.q: Both fixes pass on their own, but the checks fail when both are on the Renovate branch together. What happens?

options.text: The fixer comments on the PR that the fixes pass one by one but not together, and a person decides
options.why: Step 3 exists to catch clashes, and a clash is a decision for a person, not a reason to guess.

options.text: The fixer pushes the fixes anyway, because each one was proven
options.why: Proven alone is not proven together. The branch must be green with every bump and every fix.

options.text: The fixer pins one of the two packages back
options.why: Pinning back is never a fix; it only hides the problem until next month.

check.q: Why does Renovate open new PRs only on the 1st of the month, with releases at least 7 days old?

options.text: Because the upgrade fixers can only run once a month
options.why: The fixers run whenever a Renovate PR fails. The pace protects people, not the fixers.

options.text: Because few, grouped, slightly older updates are easier to review and less likely to bring a brand-new bug
options.why: One PR per team per month keeps attention, and the week lets others find a bad release first.

options.text: Because GitHub limits how many PRs a bot may open
options.why: The limit is our choice, made to keep dependency PRs quiet.

p: fcp gets a self-hosted Renovate (renovate.json5 at the root and .github/workflows/renovate.yml on fcp-runner-set, daily at 41 1 * * * so PRs stay rebased, new PRs only on the 1st), because Mend's hosted app cannot run postUpgradeTasks such as make -C cloud/rhinoCloud update-deps and the gRPC stub regeneration. The same PR deletes weekly-dependency-upgrades.yml and moves its gRPC version check into cloud-ci's Lint job; dependabot.yml stays for security alerts. Infrastructure and gitops get the same setup with custom regex managers for providers and chart markers.

repairGroup lives in harness/src/routines/upgrades.ts, shared by the FE and BE fixers. The fe-upgrade-fixer charter (frontend/**, a full Spot VM because flows are checked in the browser) and be-upgrade-fixer (cloud, client, sdk, with bump commands per folder and the gRPC hand-off) start in shadow; the infra upgrade fixer uses harness/scripts/verify-infra.sh and never applies. A failed Renovate PR wakes them through the trigger Action as upgrade:fcp:pr-<n>.

tickets.why: Renovate for fcp: grouped monthly PRs, 7-day release age, self-hosted, the weekly workflow removed.
Renovate for infrastructure and gitops: providers, charts and Action pins.
The FE upgrade fixer: each bump alone, one fix session per package, all together.
The BE upgrade fixer: the same pipeline for Python, with SDK and API checks.
The infra upgrade fixer: checks without credentials, and a person applies.

words.plain: The bot that opens PRs to update our dependencies; here once a month, grouped by team.
One Renovate PR that updates many packages of one area together.
The main commit a branch started from. Every bump is tried on it, alone.
How old a release must be before Renovate proposes it: 7 days for us.
A script from a package's authors that rewrites code for a new version.

review.q: From memory: the three steps of repairing a grouped update.
review.a: Try each bump alone on the base commit to find the breaking packages; one fix session per breaking package, one after another; then all fixes together on the Renovate branch before pushing.

review.q: A package cannot be fixed for its new version. What does the fixer do, and what does it never do?
review.a: It comments on the PR with what breaks and why, and leaves the decision to a person. It never pins the old version back as a fix.

remember: Renovate stays slow and grouped; when a group breaks, find the culprit by trying each bump alone, fix one package at a time, then check them all together.
